title: Trend Following Still Works — So Why Do Allocators Ignore It- - Systematic Investor - Ep.353

meta.source: Macro Transcripts/Trend Following Still Works — So Why Do Allocators Ignore It- - Systematic Investor - Ep.353.docx

speakers: Yoav Git (co-host, systematic trend-following practitioner/researcher; caption spelling 'Yov')
summary: Systematic Investor Ep.353: Niels and Yoav Git review June 2025 CTA performance and discuss four papers (negative correlation 'turbocharging', Quantica equity/trend/gold/bond mixes, SG Trend Indicator and replication, Arthur Seep on trend-following systems). Conclusion: uncorrelated trend with Sharpe similar to 60/40 deserves a large risk share; replication by correlation is meaningless; speed choice matters less than risk-scaling and portfolio diversification.

coverage.note: Disclaimer, intro; free bond data sources (MarketWatch yield curves, cbonds)
nothing actionable: AI site, book, G7, wealth report, lottery
June 2025 CTA update: volatility, short-term managers, commodities vs financials, index numbers
May experience of fast/slow switching; paper 1 (negative correlation) premise and examples
Paper 1 results; allocator constraints; types of defensive strategies
Capacity of defensive strategies, cat bonds, private equity; 50/50 trend and S&P
Zero correlation by construction; overlay on long-only assets; start of Quantica paper
Quantica design and Sharpe results for CTA, gold, bonds and the three-way mix
Diversifying the diversifiers, bond correlation caveat, 60/40 vs CTA Sharpe, risk share
SG Trend Indicator paper: industry slowing, decorrelation episodes, replication correlation
Replication meaning, indicator returns, CTA Sharpe, value of manager alpha; start of Seep paper
Seep paper history: Turtles, European school, TSMOM; secrecy and 2008 anecdotes
TSMOM, results across schools, behavioral basis, autocorrelation and drift, optimal speed
Combination with 60/40 and backtest benchmark methods (lead, noise, simulation)
Lookback weighting, volatility scaling, TSMOM optimality, diversification tilt
Fast/slow overallocation for diversification, skew, schools converge, trust in method
nothing actionable: thanks, show notes, outro

completeness_estimate: 0.88 - the first reader caught almost every argument and number in the four papers; misses were minor (G7 remark, Quantica's proxy caveat, recency-bias point, a few history and look-back remarks) and four claims in C05 look misattributed to Niels instead of Yoav.

claims.speaker: Yoav Git
claims.quote: market watch as a website uh gives you a lot of u yield curves data which is really nice and you can download the CSVs
claims.claim: MarketWatch offers downloadable yield-curve data as a free source for bond history.

claims.speaker: Yoav Git
claims.quote: the other website which you need to register but it's also very good is seabbond.com.
claims.claim: The registration-based cbonds website provides bond data including volumes and issuance.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: the daily volatility is actually pretty meaningful in the uh in the returns
claims.claim: After the April and May position changes, June 2025 trend returns showed high daily volatility and portfolios may be unevenly allocated across sectors.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: while short-term managers did well in April as from memory uh maybe even in May from memory, they're certainly catching up to u the downside uh uh to the trend followers uh in June.
claims.claim: Short-term CTAs did well in April but then fell in June, ending up on par with trend followers on a vol-adjusted basis.
claims.indicator: SG Short-Term Traders index, SG Trend index

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: commodities are doing so much better than financials this month. Uh it's really the financials that are causing a problem.
claims.claim: In June 2025 commodity sectors, especially oil after the Israel-Iran conflict, were reversing the longer downtrend and helping trend, while financial sectors were hurting it.
claims.conditions: geopolitical oil shock against prior downtrend

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: Sockchen trend up about half a percent uh down 10.8% for the year.
claims.claim: Mid-June 2025 trend indices were down for the year: BTOP50 about -3.4 percent, SG CTA -7.8, SG Trend -10.8, short-term traders -4.6, while MSCI World was +5.9 and the S&P 500 +2.3 percent near record highs; trend barometer 48 (neutral).
claims.indicator: BTOP50, SG CTA, SG Trend, SG Short-Term Traders, trend barometer

claims.speaker: Yoav Git
claims.quote: tends to switch between fast and slow momentum. So, um it was having a sort of a much better time.
claims.claim: A program that switches between fast and slow momentum had a better May 2025 than the industry average.

claims.speaker: Yoav Git
claims.quote: sometimes it's better to have a lower sharp and have a higher correlation.
claims.claim: A paper on adding negative correlation shows that for a long-term allocation an asset with lower Sharpe but low or negative correlation to the existing portfolio can add more risk-adjusted return than a higher-Sharpe asset (transcript says 'higher correlation', probably a slip).

claims.speaker: Yoav Git
claims.quote: if you have long-term uh strategy with negative correlation, you really want to even if it is losing money, even if it is flat, it will add to your risk adjusted returns
claims.claim: A negatively correlated long-term strategy improves the portfolio's risk-adjusted return even if it is flat or loses money, because it lowers overall portfolio volatility.

claims.speaker: Yoav Git
claims.quote: of the nice things about high volatility products is that they give you capital efficiency.
claims.claim: High-volatility negatively correlated strategies are capital efficient: even small allocations make a meaningful hedging impact.

claims.speaker: Yoav Git
claims.quote: even though it added, you know, less standalone expected returns, it still added quite a bit to your portfolio.
claims.claim: In the paper's two-year example, a high-vol manager with about -30 percent equity correlation but lower standalone returns added more Sharpe to an equity portfolio than a multistrat with 12 percent correlation and stronger returns.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: even if you are a mathematician and you think oh that really adds value to your portfolio you need to justify it to your investment committee.
claims.claim: Allocators face a real-world constraint: a low-Sharpe diversifier must be justified to an investment committee even when the maths says it adds value.

correction.issue: Probable wrong speaker. The speaker who lists the defensive strategies (option buying, fast trend, trend, quality) is Yoav: in C06 Niels asks 'is there anything you have come across' and Yoav answers 'the strategies that I mentioned', and Niels says 'you mentioned that there are other things'. The allocator-justification passage is part of the same unbroken paragraph.
correction.fix: Yoav Git says the real-life difficulty for an allocator is justifying a low-Sharpe diversifier to the investment committee even when the maths shows it adds value, which the paper does not address.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: fast trend has got much higher convexity and it's a little bit like buying uh buying options but with with realized volatility rather than implied volatility.
claims.claim: Fast trend following is like buying options paid for with realised rather than implied volatility, giving higher convexity as a defensive strategy.
claims.testable: yes: convexity of fast trend vs options

correction.issue: Probable wrong speaker: Yoav, the same speaker who later refers to 'the strategies that I mentioned'.
correction.fix: Yoav Git says fast trend has higher convexity and is like buying options paid for with realised rather than implied volatility.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: trend trend following is not only zero correlated to the underlying markets but also has a positive alpha.
claims.claim: Trend following sits on the boundary between hedge and alpha: zero correlated to underlying markets and with positive expected return.

correction.issue: Probable wrong speaker: Yoav; Niels's own turn begins at 'Now obviously finding a strategy...' where he says trend is not really negatively correlated.
correction.fix: Yoav Git says trend following crosses the boundary between alpha and hedge: zero correlated to underlying markets with positive alpha.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: long short equity with uh tilt towards high quality stocks
claims.claim: Long-short equity with a high-quality tilt is another defensive strategy with a long history.
claims.direction: long high quality, short low quality
claims.testable: yes: factor returns in equity drawdowns

correction.issue: Probable wrong speaker: Yoav, part of the list of defensive strategies he gives.
correction.fix: Yoav Git lists long-short equity tilted to high-quality stocks as another defensive strategy.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: We're non-correlated but we can be negative correlated at times.
claims.claim: Trend following is non-correlated to equities on average but can be negatively correlated over rolling 1 to 3 year windows, as at present.
claims.indicator: rolling correlation of trend vs equities

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: being able to uh essentially provide evidence that's not based and simulations and what have you uh is is should be uh you know uh valued quite highly.
claims.claim: A defensive strategy with a long record of actual data is more convincing to a committee than one backed by simulations.

claims.speaker: Yoav Git
claims.quote: there is a capacity because the amount of trading
claims.claim: Fast trend programs run about 1 to 2 billion and face capacity limits because of trading churn; option-based defensive strategies also have capacity limits.

claims.speaker: Yoav Git
claims.quote: you know catastrophe bonds in uh in in in my fixed income universe
claims.claim: Catastrophe bonds give return streams uncorrelated with 60/40.

claims.speaker: Yoav Git
claims.quote: I don't think that private equity is a particularly strong diversifier.
claims.claim: Private equity and private credit are not clearly diversifying because they remain exposed to the same economic factors as long equity.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: when you blend two things together, you get some kind of average. But in this case, you almost get the sum of the two.
claims.claim: A 50/50 mix of the S&P 500 and a Dunn trend program is near all-time highs, with a return close to the sum rather than the average of the two parts.

claims.speaker: Yoav Git
claims.quote: We are by construction sort of zero correlated to the assets that we trade.
claims.claim: Trend following is zero correlated to the traded assets by construction because long and short are symmetric, unlike a defensive strategy whose negative correlation may not persist.

claims.speaker: Yoav Git
claims.quote: if you try to save money and you didn't buy the put options exactly when you needed them, then when the crisis comes, you actually don't provide that
claims.claim: A tail-protect strategy only works if the puts are bought continuously; skipping them to save money removes protection at the crisis.

claims.speaker: Yoav Git
claims.quote: that gives you the power to sort of strap it on a long only exposure in Bitcoin, in gold, in equities, in bonds
claims.claim: Because trend is symmetric and zero correlated, it can be overlaid on any long-only exposure (Bitcoin, gold, equities, bonds) and stays additive.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: They look at uh the best uh 10% of equity periods. they look at the worst um uh 10% uh of equity periods
claims.claim: Quantica tests trend, gold and Treasuries as equity companions in the best and worst 10 percent of equity periods and in a 60 percent equity plus one-third each mix.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: it's not always going to be the same uh diversifying component that adds the most value to your to your equity portfolio
claims.claim: The best diversifier to equities changes by period (1990s, 2000 to 2015, last 10 years), though consistency appears over the full 1990 to 2025 sample.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: If you added instead uh uh to had a 60% equity portfolio and a 40% uh CTA uh allocation, you could increase that to 0.64 uh for your sharp.
claims.claim: From 1990 to 2025 a 60/40 equity/CTA mix lifted Sharpe from 0.49 for the S&P 500 to 0.64; gold gave 0.56.
claims.indicator: S&P 500 Sharpe, SG Trend (proxy before index)

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: the best single uh portfolio diversifier uh would have been bonds uh if you had 40% bonds um it would have gone up to 69% uh during that period
claims.claim: Bonds were the best single diversifier to equities (Sharpe 0.69 for 60/40) over 1990 to 2025.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: for the full part it was in a falling interest rate environment
claims.claim: Bonds' diversification benefit was boosted by falling interest rates through 2021, so the result may not persist.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: we now just take a third, a third, a third of gold, treasuries, and CTAs. And lo and behold, it actually delivers the best overall portfolio sharp of 72.
claims.claim: A 60 percent equity portfolio with the 40 percent split equally into gold, Treasuries and CTAs gave the best Sharpe, 0.72.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: having a diversification across your diversifier, so to speak, um, uh, across your risk mitigating strategies, I think, makes sense.
claims.claim: With regimes changing, diversifying across several liquid risk-mitigating strategies makes sense and can be implemented with ETFs.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: some people think that private equity is diversifying but to me it's still equities
claims.claim: Private equity's apparent diversification may be only lack of pricing, not true diversification.

claims.speaker: Yoav Git
claims.quote: during periods of inflation, you have you have issues about that correlation staying negative.
claims.claim: Bonds are negatively correlated with equities in falling-rate, falling-inflation periods, but the correlation is not stable during inflation.

claims.speaker: Yoav Git
claims.quote: look from 2000 onwards in the last 25 years it it only has a sharp of something like uh 0.55
claims.claim: The 60/40 portfolio had a Sharpe of about 0.76 since 1990 but only about 0.55 since 2000.

claims.speaker: Yoav Git
claims.quote: you're still looking at sharp between say 2000 and 2025 of around 0.5.
claims.claim: CTAs have a Sharpe of about 0.5 for 2000 to 2025 despite recent weakness, similar to 60/40 and uncorrelated with it.

claims.speaker: Yoav Git
claims.quote: that actually means that you should have like almost you know almost 30% of your risk in trend.
claims.claim: Even assuming a forward Sharpe of 0.7 for 60/40 and 0.3 for CTA, uncorrelated assets imply close to 30 percent of portfolio risk in trend.

claims.speaker: Yoav Git
claims.quote: a very simple implementation of a very simple trend, you know, crossover + one minus one uh indicator.
claims.claim: The SG Trend Indicator is a simple moving-average crossover with +1/-1 positions, live out of sample for 15 years.

claims.speaker: Yoav Git
claims.quote: the industry has shifted a little bit to the slow side.
claims.claim: The CTA industry has become slower: the correlation of the simple indicator run at slower speeds with the SG index rose over 15 years.
claims.indicator: correlation of simple crossover at different speeds vs SG CTA Index

correction.issue: Overstated. The speaker says the industry has shifted to the slow side, measured by the correlation of the simple indicator run at different speeds with the SG index; he does not say the correlation with slow variants rose over the 15 years.
correction.fix: Yoav Git says SG's paper shows the industry has become slower, inferred by checking which speed of the simple +1/-1 indicator correlates most with the SG index.

claims.speaker: Yoav Git
claims.quote: we can you know correlate the cot report versus different trend indicators
claims.claim: Commitments of Traders positioning vs trend indicators at different speeds also shows the industry getting slower.

claims.speaker: Yoav Git
claims.quote: during periods when there's high volatility I suspect April would would have been one covid would have been one taper tantrum would have been one
claims.claim: Trend constituents decorrelate from the simple indicator during high-vol crises (April 2025, Covid, Taper Tantrum) but converge back quickly.

claims.speaker: Yoav Git
claims.quote: without doing anything it is 80% correlated to the soj index
claims.claim: A trivial trend indicator is about 80 percent correlated with the SG CTA index, so replication papers that reach similar correlations add little.
claims.indicator: SG Trend Indicator vs SG CTA index

claims.speaker: Yoav Git
claims.quote: it's very difficult to get above 90% but it's also very difficult to get below 80%.
claims.claim: Almost any CTA is 80 to 90 percent correlated with the CTA index, unlike the 99.99 percent between SPY and the S&P 500, so replication correlation is not informative.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: since October of 2002 so more than 20 years the annualized return is 0.43%.
claims.claim: The simple SG trend indicator returned only 0.43 percent a year with 16 percent volatility (Sharpe about 0.03) since 2002 despite high correlation to the index.

claims.speaker: Yoav Git
claims.quote: we get a sharp of say4 historically and that's out of sample
claims.claim: The SG CTA Index has a Sharpe of about 0.4 out of sample after costs; good managers do better.

claims.speaker: Yoav Git
claims.quote: can we up the sharp in each of the markets that we trade just a tiny bit be it with better execution be it with some nonlinear filters be it with some some clever switching between fast and slow
claims.claim: A CTA adds value by raising Sharpe in each market slightly through execution, nonlinear filters, fast/slow switching, cost reduction and risk management.

claims.speaker: Yoav Git
claims.quote: correlation is when you remove the mean, right?
claims.claim: Correlation to a benchmark ignores the mean, so the question for a manager is the added mean return over the high-correlation, zero-alpha index.

claims.speaker: Yoav Git
claims.quote: you open a position when there's a breakout uh you wait you have a trailing stop maybe using average true range which is essentially a volatility measure
claims.claim: The American Turtle approach opens positions on breakouts and exits with an ATR trailing stop, flipping short on the reverse breakout.

claims.speaker: Yoav Git
claims.quote: a little bit more continuous change of position. It is based on moving average crossover and some volatility adjustment and risk adjustment
claims.claim: The European school (AHL and descendants) uses continuously adjusted positions from moving-average crossovers with volatility and risk scaling.
claims.indicator: moving average crossover with vol scaling

claims.speaker: Yoav Git
claims.quote: We made tons of money while everybody was losing money.
claims.claim: Trend following produced large gains in 2008 while other assets lost, an early demonstration of crisis alpha.

claims.speaker: Yoav Git
claims.quote: let's look at a yearon-year returns adjust by volatility and that's what that's what we're going to do.
claims.claim: Time-series momentum (Moskowitz-Ooi-Pedersen) takes the sign of volatility-adjusted past year return.

claims.speaker: Yoav Git
claims.quote: a lot of people are kind of very reluctant to pay for trend following despite the fact that it's very much one of the few pure alpha strategies.
claims.claim: After the TSMOM paper made trend transparent, many investors are reluctant to pay for it despite its alpha.

claims.speaker: Yoav Git
claims.quote: over the last 25 years, it really didn't matter which particular implementation you did.
claims.claim: Over the last 25 years nearly all speeds and rule types of the three trend schools made money.
claims.indicator: Turtle, European MA crossover, TSMOM at multiple speeds

claims.speaker: Yoav Git
claims.quote: trend following is a behavioral um uh sort of phenomenon is prevalent at almost all speeds and all asset classes.
claims.claim: Trend works at almost all speeds and in commodities, equities and bonds because people buy winners and sell losers.

claims.speaker: Yoav Git
claims.quote: how you are able to capture two effects. The first one is uh autocorrelation and the second thing is drift.
claims.claim: Trend returns come from capturing return autocorrelation and drift.

claims.speaker: Yoav Git
claims.quote: if I knew that the underlying process was X I knew what to speed to run but the problem is that we don't know what the problem what X is
claims.claim: The paper derives the optimal trend speed for known processes (white noise, AR(1), fractional ARMA), which gives a benchmark though the true process is unknown.

claims.speaker: Yoav Git
claims.quote: the raw sharp of the 6040 and the raw sharp of the um of the trend following strategies are actually ballpark similar and the correlation of course is zero.
claims.claim: With similar raw Sharpe and zero correlation, combining trend with 60/40 improves overall and bear-market Sharpe and the efficient frontier is easy to find.

claims.speaker: Yoav Git
claims.quote: I actually lag it in a negative fashion. I say what happens if the if the strategy knows the data ahead of time, how much money are you expected to make?
claims.claim: Test a strategy with a negative lag (look-ahead) and compare its P&L to the theoretically expected Sharpe; a mismatch signals a bug.

claims.speaker: Yoav Git
claims.quote: Suppose if I'm feeding it noise, right? If I'm feeding it noise, then I expect it to make no money.
claims.claim: Run the strategy on random noise; if some variants make money the strategy is overfitted.

claims.speaker: Yoav Git
claims.quote: I can simulate some data I can simulate the processes that we wanted to look at and we and now we understand how much am I expected to make you know with the best possible implementation.
claims.claim: Simulating known processes gives a benchmark for the best achievable performance to judge whether a new trend indicator extracts what it should.

claims.speaker: Yoav Git
claims.quote: The fact that we risk manage things properly um is is actually very powerful.
claims.claim: Volatility estimation and risk scaling was the major innovation in trend following.

claims.speaker: Yoav Git
claims.quote: even if the autocorrelations are zero or the autocorrelations are constant across the year then um then tsmon just the yearon-year returns will be optimal.
claims.claim: A 12-month TSMOM equal-weights returns and is optimal for capturing drift unless there is a strong view that autocorrelation varies through the year, so beginners can stop there.

claims.speaker: Yoav Git
claims.quote: the reason why you might want to tilt between fast and slow predictors is not necessarily to do with what they do on a standalone basis but what they do in your portfolio in terms of diversification
claims.claim: Tilt between fast and slow signals for portfolio diversification, not standalone alpha.

claims.speaker: Yoav Git
claims.quote: if I have a trend following signal which is actually negatively correlated to my to the rest of my portfolio, that's wonderful.
claims.claim: Signals that currently hedge the rest of the trend book (negative correlation) deserve more risk, which many CTAs do not do.

claims.speaker: Yoav Git
claims.quote: you might say, I actually want to overallocate to fast momentum now. Not because I necessarily think that fast momentum is a higher alpha.
claims.claim: With oil switching rapidly, overweight fast momentum in that market because it diversifies a slow-trend book, not because of higher alpha.
claims.direction: overweight fast trend in whipsaw market

claims.speaker: Yoav Git
claims.quote: If you look at the at the at this back test it will have a relatively negative negative uh skew.
claims.claim: 12-month TSMOM has little positive skew (slightly negative) while alpha is good.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: a lot of them over the very long run uh often get to pretty much the same place.
claims.claim: Breakout, moving-average and TSMOM managers end up with similar long-run performance; no evidence that one style is better.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: you're not able to follow it through thick and thin, um, it certainly won't work for you.
claims.claim: Choose a trend style you can trust and hold through bad periods, otherwise it will not work for you.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: these big institutions that we've been used to um where they you know had pretty significant power and people would listen to every single word that came out from these uh meetings.
claims.claim: Multilateral bodies such as the G7 are losing their ability to move the world, as shown by how little the June 2025 summit registered, in a world dominated by a few individuals, narratives and social media; so policy-meeting headlines carry less market-moving weight.
claims.testable: no - impressionistic judgement from one summit

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: They're looking for something with a high sharp because that's what they look for. Uh but what they really should be looking for is something that can truly derisk their portfolio
claims.claim: When improving an equity portfolio, investors typically screen candidates on standalone Sharpe, but they should look for the asset that de-risks the portfolio, for example one with negative correlation at the right time, even if its own return looks modest.
claims.indicator: standalone Sharpe vs correlation to existing portfolio
claims.direction: add a de-risking, negatively correlated asset
claims.testable: yes - compare portfolio Sharpe gains when ranking candidates by Sharpe versus by correlation-adjusted contribution

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: Now in terms of trend following they do prefer to use the socken trend index. However it doesn't exist in the 90s. So they are using a proxy for that period.
claims.claim: Quantica's 1990 to 2025 trend results rely on the SG Trend Index but use a proxy for the 1990s because the index does not exist before then, so the full-period trend Sharpe of 0.64 partly depends on a constructed series.
claims.indicator: SG Trend Index with pre-history proxy
claims.testable: yes - rerun with alternative trend proxies for the 1990s

claims.speaker: Yoav Git
claims.quote: a lot of people are looking at very recent history.
claims.claim: Investors judge trend on the last year or two, a poor stretch, and so miss its structural long-term benefit and zero correlation to a 60/40 portfolio (recency bias in manager evaluation).

claims.speaker: Yoav Git
claims.quote: completely simple completely trivial and they're not going to want to pay for us
claims.claim: Before the 2011-12 time-series momentum paper, trend managers kept their methods secret because a simple, explainable rule looks trivial and clients would then refuse to pay fees for it; transparency later made trend commonplace and harder to charge for.
claims.testable: no - industry history recollected by a former Winton/AHL staff member

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: some managers obviously you can just spread it out and say well I use 20 different look back periods and I weight them equally
claims.claim: Many trend managers diversify across look-back periods by spreading risk over about 20 horizons with equal weights, even though performance differs a lot between a 20-day and a 130 or 260-day look-back; whether a tilt across horizons adds real out-of-sample value remains an open question.
claims.conditions: equal weighting avoids look-back selection; tilting risks over-engineering that works only in backtests
claims.testable: yes - compare equal-weight and tilted look-back blends out of sample

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: a lot of the managers from the 70s, including Don, you know, started out using volatility breakout
claims.claim: Early trend managers of the 1970s used volatility breakout rules, before the price breakout of the Turtles and before moving-average and time-series momentum systems became standard, yet long-run performance records of the different styles converge.
claims.testable: partly - historical track records exist but are not public for all managers
